title: La Silla gets the green light
caption: Green airglow over La Silla Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at La Silla Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A green glow fills the sky above ESO's La Silla Observatory, on the outskirts of Chile's Atacama Desert. From left to right below it stand the 3.6m telescope and New Technology Telescope, both ESO's, then the Swiss 1.2-metre Leonhard Euler Telescope.

The glow is airglow, faint light given off by Earth's atmosphere. It is invisible to the naked eye, but sensitive cameras can record it in very dark places with little light pollution, like this one. Ultraviolet radiation from the Sun sets off chemical processes that make atoms in the upper atmosphere shine very weakly. This green comes from oxygen atoms, while other atoms or molecules can make it red or yellow.

Airglow should not be mistaken for an aurora. Auroras are fleeting, shifting displays caused by charged particles flung into Earth's magnetic field, while airglow is always there, more like quiet background music.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based photograph by J. Pérez taken with a sensitive camera. The source does not publish exposure or colour-processing details.
understand.eye: Airglow is invisible to the naked eye, and only a sensitive camera picks up its green light.

explore: The telescopes can be visited in person. Tours take place during the day so they do not disturb the night's work, which means no airglow, but ESO says the telescopes more than make up for it.
alt: A green glow across a starry sky above three telescope buildings.
